CausalChain: Gut microbiota modulates bile acid profiles -> Altered bile acid composition shifts the balance between hydrophobic (e.g., DCA, LCA) and hydrophilic bile acids (e.g., UDCA) -> Differential binding to nuclear and membrane receptors (FXR, TGR5, PXR, VDR) in cancer cells -> Activation of distinct downstream signaling cascades (e.g., pro-apoptotic, anti-inflammatory, metabolic reprogramming) -> Modulation of cancer stem cell properties and immune microenvironment
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that modulation of gut microbiota to favor the production of hydrophilic bile acids, such as UDCA, can reprogram the bile acid receptor signaling in breast cancer cells toward a tumor suppressive state by altering cellular metabolism and reducing cancer stem cell features, thereby enhancing the response to conventional therapies.
Abstract: Recent studies have emphasized the pleiotropic roles of bile acids in carcinogenesis, where they act as not only digestive agents but also potent signaling molecules that modulate inflammatory, metabolic, and apoptotic pathways through a variety of receptors such as FXR, TGR5, PXR, and VDR. Emerging data suggest that bile acid composition, which is largely determined by gut microbial metabolism, plays a dual role in cancer progression depending on both the concentration and the specific receptor context in target tissues. In this review, we propose a novel hypothesis in which modulation of bile acid receptor signaling states via gut-microbiome‐driven alterations in bile acid composition governs a reversible switch between tumor suppressive and tumor promoting phenotypes. In particular, the interplay between hydrophilic bile acids such as ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) and the expression profile of receptors like FXR and TGR5 in breast cancer cells may reprogram cellular metabolism and enhance anti‐tumor immune responses. Through controlled microbial fermentation, specific bile acid profiles can be induced, shifting the signaling balance toward tumor suppressive pathways and possibly enhancing the efficacy of chemotherapeutic agents.
